passage: It was the last week of the quarter at the insurance office in Mohali, and Avni, the unpaid intern, was building Baljeet's client report for the third time that month while he watched cricket highlights at his desk. Her jaw ached from clenching. By 8 p.m. a small, mean idea arrived: leave one wrong total in his report and let the manager catch him. She stared at the cell. Then she saved the file correctly and wrote three lines on a sticky note instead: what she had been asked to do as an intern, what she had actually been doing, and what she wanted to learn. Not every office would be like this one, she reminded herself. The next morning, with the deadline still pressing on everyone, she asked the manager, Mrs. Arora, for ten minutes. 'I'm glad to help the team, but I've been writing Baljeet's reports. I'd like my own project, and a clear idea of what's mine.' Mrs. Arora raised her eyebrows, then asked for the list.

qa.q: What was Baljeet watching at his desk?
qa.a: Baljeet was watching cricket highlights.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling as she stared at the cell?
qa.a: Avni felt resentful and bitter, tempted to plant a wrong total to get back at Baljeet.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Saving the file correctly and asking Mrs. Arora for her own project and clear scope, because it named the unfairness without sabotage.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Arora see Avni's request?
qa.a: Mrs. Arora seems surprised but takes it seriously by asking for the list, which suggests she may not have known how much Avni was covering.

grounding: Shows an intern seething while covering a staff member's work for free, resisting sabotage, and instead naming the unfairness and negotiating her scope.

passage: By his sixth week as an unpaid intern at a Bengaluru software firm, Kishore had fixed three bugs assigned to Shalini, a full-time developer who left at five every day. The first time he felt proud. The third time he felt something darker. He began answering her messages with one-word replies, taking long lunches to make her wait, and telling friends that 'all offices are scams run by lazy people'. On Saturday his father, who had worked thirty years at a bus depot, listened and said, 'Some places are like that. Not all. Don't let one bad plate spoil your appetite.' On Monday Kishore dropped the silent treatment. He went to his mentor, listed the tickets he had done that weren't his, and asked for his own module and a clear scope. The mentor agreed, and made a note about Shalini's tickets too. Kishore kept the bug fixes in his portfolio.

qa.q: How many of Shalini's bugs had Kishore fixed?
qa.a: Kishore had fixed three bugs assigned to Shalini.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling by the third bug?
qa.a: Kishore felt resentful and bitter, which came out as quiet spite and cynicism about all offices.

qa.q: What did Kishore do on Monday that worked better than spite?
qa.a: He listed the tickets that weren't his, asked his mentor for his own module and scope, and kept the work for his portfolio.

qa.q: How does Kishore's father see the situation?
qa.a: Kishore's father sees it as one bad workplace, not proof that all work is unfair.

grounding: Shows an intern's resentment at covering a full-timer's work turning into quiet spite, then being redirected into naming the problem and negotiating scope.

passage: I'm Manjula, and I didn't expect my best memory of that internship to be the pantry. There were six of us interns at the ad agency in Mumbai, and in the first month we mostly competed: who stayed later, who got noticed. Payal was the one who changed it. She started a small group chat where we swapped tips: which manager wanted short emails, how to leave before midnight without looking lazy, who could cover a task if someone's train was late. When I had a fever, two of them finished my storyboards. By the second month we'd all noticed the same thing: six of us working twelve-hour days on a stipend that didn't cover travel. Nobody wanted to complain alone. So we wrote one polite email together, with our hours listed, and asked for a meeting with HR. They raised the travel allowance and set an 8 p.m. cutoff for interns. We still have that group chat.

qa.q: How many interns were at the agency?
qa.a: There were six interns at the agency.

qa.q: How does Manjula seem to feel looking back on the group?
qa.a: Manjula feels warm and grateful, remembering the group as the best part of the internship.

qa.q: Why did writing one email together work?
qa.a: It showed a shared problem with listed hours, so no one had to complain alone, and HR responded with a travel allowance and a cutoff.

qa.q: What might Payal have wanted when she started the group chat?
qa.a: Payal likely wanted the interns to help each other rather than compete, which made everyone's days easier.

grounding: A first-person account of interns moving from competing to covering for each other, and using that solidarity to raise hours and pay together.

passage: Supervisor's note, front office internship, Week 5. Something worth recording. On Tuesday the duty manager hinted to the interns that whoever 'reported problems' in the team would get the permanent offer. I expected tale-telling. Instead, Gargi came to me with Dolma, the two of them nervous but together. They had a list, signed by all four interns: double shifts on three weekends, no meal breaks on two of them, and a question about the stipend being paid late. Gargi did most of the talking; Dolma had the dates. Neither said a word against the other, though I know Dolma has been late twice because of her bus. I told them the list was fair and that I would take it to the HR head myself. I did so the same afternoon. I also told the duty manager that setting interns against each other stops today.

qa.q: How many interns signed the list?
qa.a: All four interns signed the list.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling as she came in with Dolma?
qa.a: Gargi was nervous, but steadier for having Dolma and the others behind her.

qa.q: Why was the interns' approach stronger than tale-telling?
qa.a: They raised shared concerns with dates and signatures instead of informing on each other, so the supervisor could act on facts.

qa.q: What would change for Dolma if Gargi had reported her lateness to win the offer?
qa.a: Dolma could have lost her chance, and the interns would have been divided instead of standing together.

grounding: A supervisor's note records interns choosing solidarity over informing on each other, and raising hours and pay concerns together.

passage: At Sunday lunch in Lisbon, Sami's mother, Rosa, was telling his aunts again: 'He works at the big consulting firm downtown now, in the glass tower.' Sami smiled and passed the bread. What he didn't say: he was an unpaid intern who mostly booked meeting rooms and printed slides, and he took two buses because the firm didn't cover transport. Every time she said 'consultant', the gap in his chest widened. That evening, drying dishes, he said it. 'Mãe, I need to tell you something. I'm an intern there, not staff. It's unpaid, and a lot of it is admin.' She put the plate down slowly. 'Then why did you let me say it?' 'Because you looked so proud.' He told her what he was learning, how to structure a report, how meetings run, and that he'd apply for paid junior roles in March. She was quiet. Then: 'I'm still proud. Just of the true thing.'

qa.q: What did Sami mostly do at the firm?
qa.a: Sami mostly booked meeting rooms and printed slides.

qa.q: What was Sami feeling when his mother said 'consultant'?
qa.a: Sami felt guilty and uncomfortable, the gap between her pride and the truth widening.

qa.q: What made Sami's way of telling the truth wise?
qa.a: He told her gently and privately, and explained what he was learning and his plan to apply for paid roles in March.

qa.q: How does Rosa take the truth?
qa.a: Rosa is surprised and a little hurt that Sami let her say it, but stays proud of the true thing.

grounding: Shows a mother proudly overstating an unpaid internship, and Sami closing the guilty gap by gently telling the truth along with his learning and plans.

passage: Binita's father had taken a half-day from the bank to visit her 'office' in Kolkata's Salt Lake tech park, a box of sandesh in his hands for her 'colleagues'. He had already told the whole family chat that his daughter worked at a multinational. In the marble lobby, waiting for a visitor pass, Binita felt sick. She was one of twenty unpaid trainees in a basement room, labelling data eight hours a day. She took her father to the lobby café first. 'Baba, before we go up, I need to tell you. I'm a trainee, not an employee. There's no salary yet.' Tarun blinked. 'But you said...' 'I said I work here. I let you think the rest. I'm sorry.' She showed him her notebook: the labelling rules she had learned, the coding course she did in the evenings, the two paid roles she had applied for. Her father looked at the sandesh box. 'Then let's give these to the other trainees.'

qa.q: What was Binita's father carrying?
qa.a: Binita's father was carrying a box of sandesh.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling in the marble lobby?
qa.a: Binita felt sick with guilt, knowing her father believed she worked at a multinational.

qa.q: What did Binita do that closed the gap?
qa.a: She told him the truth privately before going up, apologised, and showed what she was learning and the roles she had applied for.

qa.q: What does Tarun's offer to give the sweets to the other trainees suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he accepts the truth and is still proud, choosing to share the moment with the trainees.

grounding: Shows a proud father who believes his daughter has a big-firm job, and Binita gently telling the truth about being an unpaid trainee along with her plans.

passage: Leila had been delivering by scooter in Mexico City for eight months when two things happened in one week. The app lowered the base rate per trip without any message, and on Friday her account was blocked: 'Unusual activity detected.' There was no phone number, only a chat bot that repeated the same sentence. She sat on the curb outside a taquería, helmet still on, feeling like she was arguing with a wall. Santiago, who rode for the same app, found her there. 'Screenshot everything. The block, the old rate, the new rate.' He added her to the riders' group that met on Wednesdays and had a volunteer who helped with appeals. That night Leila wrote down, for the first time, what she really made in a week after fuel. It was less than she had thought. On Monday her account came back. She kept the notebook, and she asked her cousin about weekend shifts at his bakery.

qa.q: How long had Leila been delivering?
qa.a: Leila had been delivering for eight months.

qa.q: What was Leila feeling on the curb?
qa.a: Leila felt powerless and frustrated, like she was arguing with a wall.

qa.q: Which steps helped Leila, and why?
qa.a: Screenshots and the riders' group gave her evidence and support for the appeal, while tracking earnings after fuel and asking about bakery shifts built other options.

qa.q: How does Santiago see Leila's situation?
qa.a: Santiago recognises it as a common problem for riders and knows the steps, so he offers practical help.

grounding: Shows a rider facing a silent rate cut and an unexplained block, and the steps of keeping screenshots, joining a workers' group, tracking real earnings and building other income.

passage: The workers' help desk at the community centre in Hyderabad opened at 6 p.m. on Thursdays, and Harish arrived at 5:40 with his phone fully charged. For two weeks the ride app had been paying him less per kilometre, and on Monday it had suspended him for 'low acceptance', though he had only refused rides at night on a road he knew was unsafe. Madhuri, a law student who volunteered at the desk, didn't promise anything. 'First, the screenshots. Every rate notice, every suspension message.' He had some; together they found the rest in his email. Madhuri added his case to the group complaint the drivers' union was preparing. Then came the question, 'How much do you make in a day after fuel?' He didn't know. Madhuri gave him a small notebook to write it down each night. Walking out, Harish felt less alone than he had in weeks, and texted his cousin about the evening job at the grocery store.

qa.q: At what time does the help desk open on Thursdays?
qa.a: The help desk opens at 6 p.m. on Thursdays.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling as he walked out of the help desk?
qa.a: Harish felt less alone than he had in weeks, after feeling powerless against the app.

qa.q: What steps did Madhuri help Harish take?
qa.a: Collecting screenshots, joining the union's group complaint and tracking daily earnings after fuel, while he looked into other work.

qa.q: How does Madhuri approach Harish's problem?
qa.a: Madhuri is careful not to promise anything, and focuses on practical steps and joining others in the complaint.

grounding: Shows a driver cut and suspended by an app with no human contact, and a help desk guiding him to records, a workers' group, real earnings and other income.

passage: The office tower in Gurugram had a front desk, a metal detector and a rule that riders wait by the side door. Rafiq reached it at 1:03 p.m. for a 1:00 lunch order, soaked from a sudden shower. The customer came down, took the bag without looking at him and said, 'Three minutes. Do you people even own watches? I'm giving you one star.' Then he walked off, still talking on his phone. Rafiq stood by the side door feeling like a piece of furniture. His face burned. Sudha, the security guard at the desk, had seen it all. 'He does that to every rider,' she said quietly, and handed him a paper towel for his wet hands. Rafiq breathed out slowly. He opened the app and used the report option to note the rain and the abuse, calm and factual. Then he checked his next order. The rudeness had been about that man, not about him.

qa.q: At what time did Rafiq reach the tower?
qa.a: Rafiq reached it at 1:03 p.m.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling at the side door?
qa.a: Rafiq felt invisible and humiliated, like a piece of furniture, his face burning.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do that kept his dignity?
qa.a: He stayed calm, breathed, used the app's report option with facts, and moved on to the next order.

qa.q: How does Sudha see the customer's behaviour?
qa.a: Sudha sees it as a habit he shows every rider, not something about Rafiq.

grounding: Shows a rider scolded for being three minutes late by a customer who won't look at him, and his calm, dignified use of the report tools.

passage:
Dear Rehana-di,
You asked on the phone why I sounded quiet. Here's the honest answer. Yesterday I delivered biryani to a flat in Whitefield. I was three minutes late because the society guard made me show my ID twice. The man who opened the door didn't look at me once. He said, 'Useless,' to the air above my head and shut the door. I stood in that corridor with the empty bag, feeling like I didn't exist.
I wanted to ring the bell again and shout. I didn't. I walked down, sat on my bike, and counted ten breaths the way you taught me before exams. Then I used the report button in the app and wrote exactly what happened, no bad words.
I've decided that man's rudeness is his problem, not a verdict on me. I still feel the sting a bit. But I'm eating properly, and I'm back on the road.
Your brother,
Darshan

qa.q: Why was Darshan three minutes late?
qa.a: The society guard made Darshan show the ID twice.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling in the corridor with the empty bag?
qa.a: Darshan felt invisible and hurt, as if he didn't exist.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Counting ten breaths and using the report button with facts instead of shouting, because it kept his dignity and created a record.

qa.q: How might Rehana-di feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Rehana-di would likely feel sad for her brother but proud that he stayed calm and used her breathing trick.

grounding: A letter shows a delivery rider treated with contempt at a door, staying calm, using the report tools and deciding the rudeness says nothing about his worth.

passage: It was 44 degrees in Nagpur, and by his eleventh delivery Arnab's shirt was stuck to his back. The last drop that afternoon was a parcel for the reception of a small eye clinic. The receptionist, Shreya, signed for it, then paused. 'Wait.' She came back with a steel glass of cold water and a paper cup of nimbu pani. 'Take care on the road, bhaiya. It's brutal out there.' Arnab drank both standing by the counter, and for a second his throat closed, not from thirst. Nobody had looked him in the eye all day. He thanked her twice. On his way out, he held the door for an old man with a patch over one eye and helped him down the steps to his auto. Riding off, Arnab caught himself humming. Kind or rude, he thought, people at the door were having their own days; he was still the same rider either way.

qa.q: What did Shreya bring Arnab?
qa.a: Shreya brought a steel glass of cold water and a paper cup of nimbu pani.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when Shreya offered the water?
qa.a: Arnab felt touched and moved, since nobody had looked him in the eye all day.

qa.q: How did Arnab pass the kindness on?
qa.a: He held the door for an old man and helped him down the steps to his auto.

qa.q: What might Shreya have been thinking when she said 'Wait'?
qa.a: Shreya probably noticed how hot and tired Arnab looked and wanted to show some care.

grounding: Shows a small kindness to a delivery rider lifting his day, his passing it on, and his sense that strangers' moods do not set his worth.

passage:
Dear Ira,
You'll laugh, but a bottle of water made my week.
Wednesday was awful. Rain, two wrong addresses, and a customer who told me girls shouldn't do this job. By the last order I was shaking with tiredness. It was a small house in Kothrud. An auntie opened the door, took the parcel, and then handed me a cold bottle of water and a packet of biscuits. 'Take care on the road, beta,' she said. That's all. I nearly cried on her doorstep.
I've been thinking about it since. I don't want to decide how I feel about myself by who is rude or kind at a door. But I can choose what I pass on. Today I let a rider go ahead of me at the petrol pump because he looked more tired than me, and I bought the chai stall's last two cups for the two of us.
Your friend always,
Hafsa

qa.q: Where was the small house?
qa.a: The small house was in Kothrud.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling on the auntie's doorstep?
qa.a: Hafsa felt touched and close to tears after an exhausting, insulting day.

qa.q: How did Hafsa pass the kindness on?
qa.a: She let a tired rider go ahead at the petrol pump and bought chai for the two of them.

qa.q: What might the auntie have noticed about Hafsa?
qa.a: The auntie probably saw how tired Hafsa was in the rain and wanted to show simple care.

grounding: A letter shows a customer's small kindness brightening a rider's hard day, and her choosing to pass it on without letting strangers decide her worth.

passage: You want to know my worst week? I'm Sharmila, and last March I rode eleven, twelve hours a day on my scooter, chasing the weekly bonus. The app kept showing a little bar: 'Just 6 more trips to unlock!' So I'd do six more. Then it would say '4 more for the next level.' My friend Jasleen rode too, and one night she found me asleep on my scooter seat outside a mall at 1 a.m., helmet still on. She shook me awake and made me sit on the kerb. Then she took my phone and did the maths with me: money that week, minus fuel, divided by the hours. It came to less per hour than her bakery counter job paid. I felt stupid, and then angry. Those bars were built to keep me riding. Now I stop at nine hours, bonus or no bonus. Riding half-asleep wasn't worth any level on that bar.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen find Sharmila asleep?
qa.a: Jasleen found Sharmila asleep on the scooter seat outside a mall at 1 a.m.

qa.q: What did Sharmila feel once the maths was done?
qa.a: Sharmila felt foolish and then angry, realising the bonus bars were built to keep riders going.

qa.q: What change did Sharmila make, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Sharmila now stops at nine hours whatever the bonus, because riding exhausted is dangerous and the long hours didn't pay off.

qa.q: What was it like for Jasleen to find Sharmila asleep on the scooter?
qa.a: Jasleen was probably frightened for Sharmila's safety, which is why she woke her, sat her down and did the maths with her.

grounding: A spoken account of riding eleven-hour days for incentive targets, working out the real hourly pay, and choosing rest over exhausted riding.

passage:
Monday: Harsha logged in at 8 a.m. and was still riding at 9 p.m., chasing the 'weekend warrior' bonus the app had flashed that morning. His eyes stung. At a red light in Koramangala, his head dipped for a second and a car horn jolted him awake.
Wednesday: At the tea stall, Harsha told Asif about the horn. Asif didn't laugh. He pulled out a small notebook where he had written his real numbers for a month: money earned, fuel, hours. 'Divide it. Then decide if the bonus is worth sleeping at a signal.' Harsha did his own sums that night on the back of a receipt. The long days paid less per hour than he had thought.
The next Monday: Harsha set an alarm for nine hours online and logged off when it rang, even with a bonus bar half full. He slept eight hours for the first time in weeks. The bar reset. He didn't chase it.

qa.q: Where did Harsha's head dip at a red light?
qa.a: Harsha's head dipped at a red light in Koramangala.

qa.q: What was Harsha likely feeling after the car horn jolted him awake?
qa.a: Harsha was probably shaken and scared, realising how exhausted he had become.

qa.q: What did Harsha change after doing the sums?
qa.a: Seeing that long days paid less per hour than he thought, he now logs off after nine hours even with a bonus bar half full.

qa.q: Why didn't Asif laugh at the story about the horn?
qa.a: Asif took it as a real danger and wanted Harsha to see the true numbers before he got hurt.

grounding: Shows a rider hooked on incentive targets until a near-miss, then working out his real hourly earnings and choosing rest.

passage: The kebab kiosk near Warsaw's central station was where the riders waited between orders, and in his first winter Ivan learned more there than from the app. Amara, from Lagos, showed him which bridge iced over first. An older rider warned everyone about an address where a customer grabbed at bags. When Ivan's chain snapped at 10 p.m., three riders appeared with tools and a torch. He had moved from Kharkiv knowing nobody; now there was a place where people knew his name. One night, over cheap coffee, Amara said, 'We all lost the rain bonus this month. One complaint gets ignored. Thirty doesn't.' Ivan offered to set up a group chat and collect everyone's screenshots. By Sunday there were twenty-six riders in it and a draft letter to the company, polite and signed by all of them. Ivan read it twice and felt, for the first time in Poland, part of something.

qa.q: When did Ivan's chain snap?
qa.a: Ivan's chain snapped at 10 p.m.

qa.q: What does Ivan feel about the riders at the kiosk?
qa.a: Ivan feels grateful and at home, having come from Kharkiv knowing nobody and now having people who know his name.

qa.q: How did the riders use their network beyond helping each other?
qa.a: They collected screenshots and signed a polite joint letter to the company about the lost rain bonus.

qa.q: Why might Amara think thirty complaints matter more than one?
qa.a: Amara seems to have seen single complaints ignored, and believes a group is harder for the company to dismiss.

grounding: Shows riders sharing routes, warnings and repairs, the belonging it creates, and the network being used to ask for better terms together.

passage: In the waiting room of the grocery dark store in Pune, the riders kept a whiteboard nobody had officially allowed. Chetan had started it in his second month: 'Flooded: Sinhagad Road underpass', 'Dog pack: Lane 7', 'Customer at B-wing asks for OTP twice, be careful.' Suraj, the newest rider, read it on his first day and laughed. By his third day he was adding to it. When Suraj's tyre went flat in the monsoon, Chetan and two others found a spare tube and fixed it in the parking lot in ten minutes. Suraj felt, for the first time since leaving Latur, that he had people. Then the store cut the per-order rate. The riders gathered by the whiteboard. 'Nobody goes alone to the store manager,' Chetan said. 'We go together, with our order slips.' The next morning eighteen riders stood outside the manager's glass cabin, calm, slips in hand. The manager agreed to a meeting on Friday.

qa.q: What did the whiteboard say about Lane 7?
qa.a: The whiteboard said 'Dog pack: Lane 7'.

qa.q: What did Suraj feel after the riders fixed his tyre?
qa.a: Suraj felt grateful and relieved, sensing he had people for the first time since leaving Latur.

qa.q: Why was going to the manager together wise?
qa.a: A calm group with order slips is harder to ignore than one rider, and nobody gets singled out.

qa.q: What might Chetan have wanted when he started the whiteboard?
qa.a: Chetan likely wanted riders to keep each other safe and informed, which later made standing together easier.

grounding: Shows riders at a dark store sharing warnings and help, a newcomer finding belonging, and the group going together to ask for better terms.

passage: At his cousin Tanuja's engagement in Jalandhar, Baljeet kept his phone face down so no one would see the delivery app's orange screen. When Tayaji asked what he was doing these days, he said, 'Something in logistics,' and steered the talk to cricket. He had been riding for four months since his engineering results came out badly, and every lie made him feel smaller. Then, halfway through dinner, his phone chimed loudly: 'Your pickup is ready.' Tanuja, sitting next to him, glanced at the screen. Later, by the sweets table, she said quietly, 'You deliver food? Why hide it?' 'Because they'll say I've fallen.' 'You're paying for your re-exam yourself. That's not falling.' Before leaving, Baljeet told Tayaji the truth, and his plan: ride until the re-exam in June, then apply for site engineer jobs. Tayaji grunted, then said, 'Good. Honest work.' His face still burned, but less.

qa.q: What did Baljeet first tell Tayaji he was doing?
qa.a: Baljeet said, 'Something in logistics.'

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel each time he lied?
qa.a: Baljeet felt smaller and ashamed, afraid relatives would say he had fallen.

qa.q: What made Baljeet's final answer to Tayaji wise?
qa.a: He told the truth and shared a clear plan: riding until the June re-exam, then applying for site engineer jobs.

qa.q: How does Tanuja see Baljeet's job?
qa.a: Tanuja sees it as honest work that pays for his re-exam, not a fall.

grounding: Shows a young man hiding food-delivery work from relatives out of shame, then explaining it honestly with a plan and timeline.

passage: For three months Zainab had told her Khala and cousins in Lucknow that she worked at a call centre. In truth she delivered groceries on her scooter across Gomti Nagar, in a helmet that hid her face when she passed their street. The money paid for her typing course. But the lie had a cost: she had stopped going to the course on Saturdays in case a cousin saw her near the institute. On Friday her friend Anand, who rode for the same company, asked why she had missed class twice. 'In case someone sees me in the uniform,' she said. Anand shrugged. 'Your Khala sells pickles from home. Is that low?' Zainab laughed despite herself. That night at dinner she told Khala everything: the scooter, the money, the typing course, the plan to apply for office jobs by December. Khala was quiet, then said, 'Next time you're in our lane, stop for tea.' On Saturday Zainab went to class.

qa.q: What had Zainab told her Khala she did?
qa.a: Zainab had said she worked at a call centre.

qa.q: What was Zainab afraid of when she skipped the Saturday class?
qa.a: Zainab was afraid and ashamed that a cousin might see her in the delivery uniform.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Telling Khala the truth and the December plan, because it ended the lie and let her return to the course that was the point of the work.

qa.q: How does Anand see Zainab's worry about status?
qa.a: Anand sees nothing low in honest work and gently points out that Zainab's Khala also works from home.

grounding: Shows the private sting of hiding delivery work from relatives, the lie starting to stall her progress, and honesty about the plan setting it right.

passage: The offer came from the small school in Sohra where Disha had done her teaching practice. The principal, Elizabeth, told her the salary on the phone and added, 'Let me know by Friday.' It was lower than Disha had hoped. That evening she sat by the stove in her aunt's house and felt her stomach knot. If she asked for more, would they just give the job to someone else? Her aunt, who had taught for twenty years, said, 'Don't guess. Find out.' Disha called two classmates teaching at similar schools nearby and checked the pay in three job notices in town. Her offer was at the bottom. On Thursday she called the principal, voice shaking slightly: 'I'm very happy to accept. Given my practice term with you and the range at similar schools, could the salary be a little closer to the middle?' A pause. 'Let me speak to the board.' Disha put the phone down and breathed out. Whatever came back, she had decided, she would take the job.

qa.q: By when did the principal want an answer?
qa.a: The principal wanted an answer by Friday.

qa.q: What was Disha afraid of as she sat by the stove?
qa.a: Disha was afraid that asking for more would make them give the job to someone else.

qa.q: What steps made Disha's request reasonable?
qa.a: She checked pay with classmates and job notices, asked politely with reasons, and was ready to accept whatever the board decided.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth see Disha's call?
qa.a: Elizabeth seems to take it as a fair request, promising to speak to the board rather than withdrawing the offer.

grounding: Shows the fear that asking for more will lose an offer, and Disha researching the range, asking politely with reasons and being ready to accept the answer.

passage: Wei had the offer email open on her laptop in her Toronto dorm for two days without replying. The junior analyst role was exactly what she wanted. The salary was lower than the figures she had seen for the same title on two salary-survey sites and in her university's graduate report. Every time she started typing a question, she pictured Zeynep, the hiring manager, frowning and saying, 'Never mind, then.' Her roommate finally sat on the bed. 'What's the worst realistic answer?' 'They say no.' 'And then?' 'I take it anyway.' 'So you lose nothing by asking.' Wei wrote a short, polite email: thanks, excitement, the ranges she had found, and a request to move closer to the middle. She sent it before she could delete it. Zeynep replied the next afternoon: the band was fixed for new graduates, but they could add a pay review at six months. Wei felt a flicker of disappointment, and accepted.

qa.q: How long did Wei leave the offer email without replying?
qa.a: Wei left it for two days.

qa.q: What was Wei afraid of while the email sat unanswered?
qa.a: Wei was afraid Zeynep would withdraw the offer and say 'Never mind, then.'

qa.q: Why was Wei's email a sound approach?
qa.a: It was polite and based on the ranges she had researched, and she was ready to accept whatever the answer was.

qa.q: How does Zeynep respond to Wei's request?
qa.a: Zeynep doesn't withdraw the offer; the reply explains the fixed band and offers a six-month review instead.

grounding: Shows fear of losing an offer by negotiating, and Wei researching the range, asking politely and accepting the answer she gets.
